name: PT Bank China Construction Bank Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: CCB Indonesia: a well-capitalised bank that earns less than its cost of equity
frontmatter.summary: CCB Indonesia trades at a fraction of book because it earns far less than its cost of equity, and the discount is earned rather than a mispricing. Deposits ran off while loans grew, repo replaced deposits, fee income halved, and provisioning runs below the migration visible in watchlist loans. Our target is Rp43 against Rp57, a -22.0% total return, and we rate the shares REDUCE.
thesis: The funding model broke in the first nine months of the year: third-party deposits fell by more than a tenth while gross loans still grew, and the gap was filled with interbank deposits and repo, not with cheap current accounts [S4]. A bank that funds corporate loans with wholesale money has no margin buffer when rates stay flat.

Profitability is structurally below the cost of equity, not temporarily depressed. Net interest margin fell from 3.0% in FY2025 on the bank's own definition, from a much higher level two years earlier, and the nine-month run-rate is lower again; fee income halved year on year and operating costs kept growing [S4, S5].

The balance sheet looks clean at the headline ratio, but provisioning is running at a fraction of the prior year's charge while watchlist loans rose and the allowance covers only part of the impaired pool; we model a normalised charge well above the nine-month run-rate [S4, S5].

Capital is not the constraint and it is not being used: common equity tier one of 26.7% on risk-weighted assets of IDR25,075.2bn against a 9.0%-10.0% requirement leaves a surplus larger than the company's entire market capitalisation, yet nothing has been distributed since the 2007 listing and the payout policy is a ceiling, not a commitment. The surplus earns the same sub-cost return as the rest of the book, so at cost of equity it destroys value rather than creating it; it is the one event that could re-rate the shares, and we carry it explicitly - the base case prices it at the same fraction of par that the justified multiple applies to book, and the bull at a materially higher proportion [S4, S5].

At Rp57 the shares trade at 0.3x FY2026E book and 7.7x FY2026E earnings; on a sustainable return on equity of 3.5% against a cost of equity of 11.85% the warranted P/BV is 0.30 times book, so the operating return the price embeds is close to the one we think the bank can earn - the disagreement is the probability and timing of the surplus capital coming back, and the illiquidity haircut, not the margin or the credit charge [S0, S4, S5].

The stock is illiquid - three-month average daily turnover of IDR278.9m against a market capitalisation of IDR2,161.4bn - so a REDUCE view is a valuation call, not a trade most holders can express at size [S0].

blocks.text: We initiate on Bank China Construction Bank Indonesia (MCOR) with a **REDUCE** rating and a target of **Rp43**, -22.0% below the Rp57 close. The company is the Indonesian subsidiary of China Construction Bank, a corporate and small-business lender with a treasury book almost as large as its loan book, and it is priced at 0.3x FY2026E book and 7.7x FY2026E earnings. Our view is not that the bank is badly run. It is that the bank earns a return on equity of 4.3% on our FY2025 numbers, against a cost of equity of 11.85%, and nothing in the last nine months of disclosure changes that arithmetic [S4, S5].

The variant view is about the direction of the discount, not its existence. A bank earning below its cost of equity is worth less than its book, and the market already pays less than a third of book. What the price still embeds is an option that the franchise returns to a mid-single-digit return on equity, funded by a controller who has never paid a dividend, or that the controlling shareholder eventually buys in the minority at a premium. We cannot source either. The one genuinely new positive is the designation of the bank as a placement bank for natural-resource export proceeds, which could rebuild the FX deposit base that left during the year, and we carry it in the bull case rather than the base [S2].

Three things move the value. First, the funding base: third-party deposits fell from Rp28,666.0bn at end-2025 to Rp25,081.1bn at 30 September 2026, while gross loans rose to Rp27,351.9bn [S4]. The gap was funded by deposits from other banks of Rp3,009.3bn and repo liabilities of Rp3,531.6bn, both far above their year-end levels, and wholesale funding is the most expensive and least stable liability a small bank can carry [S4]. Second, the margin: net interest margin was 3.0% in FY2025 on the bank's definition and the nine-month run is lower, with the model at 2.6% for the year, because the asset yield fell faster than the funding cost [S4, S5]. Third, credit: the gross non-performing loan ratio improved to 1.4%, but watchlist loans rose from Rp496.3bn to Rp699.0bn in nine months and the allowance against impaired loans is only Rp114.0bn against Rp373.3bn of stage-three exposure [S4].

The valuation is built from one set of assumptions, and that is the change the review asked for. We weight residual income and warranted P/BV equally - the bank card's engine and its cross-check - and we drop the dividend discount model because the payout is policy-capped near term, so it would capitalise a limited stream rather than the franchise [S0, S5]. Both legs run off the same payout path: the stated policy ceiling of 20.0% in the explicit years, then a full distribution of earnings in the terminal state, at which the method's own constraint makes terminal growth 0.0%. Warranted P/BV at a sustainable return on equity of 3.5% and a cost of equity of 11.85% gives 0.30 times book, or Rp57; residual income, which discounts the model's own negative excess returns on the same path, gives Rp41 [S0]. The blend is Rp49; capitalised one year at the cost of equity it is Rp54, the bear and bull paths give Rp38 and Rp69, and the probability-weighted value before the liquidity discount is Rp54. The house discount of 20% for thin turnover takes the target to Rp43 [S0]. The surplus capital is carried inside that target at the fraction of par the multiple implies, stated and sourced in the valuation section; it is the single largest swing in the name, and the price still embeds a more generous view of it than we do.

MCOR is PT Bank China Construction Bank Indonesia Tbk, a commercial bank listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and controlled by China Construction Bank Corporation with a 60.0% stake [S5]. It lends to corporates, to commercial and small and medium-sized enterprises, and to consumers, and it runs a treasury and securities book that is large relative to the loan book: earning assets were Rp36,701.6bn at end-2025 against gross loans of Rp26,407.2bn [S5]. The bank employed 1,081 people at the last count and operates from Jakarta with branches in Bandung, Semarang, Yogyakarta, Surabaya, Denpasar, Mataram, Palembang, Bandar Lampung, Batam, Pekanbaru, Pontianak, Makassar and Pangkal Pinang [S0, S5].

The business model is a corporate and commercial spread business with a transaction-banking overlay. Loans are funded by customer deposits, interbank deposits and repo, and the bank holds a securities portfolio that produces interest income and provides collateral for the repo funding it uses when deposits are short [S4]. That structure explains both the margin and its sensitivity: the loan book is corporate-weighted, so yields are negotiated rather than priced off a retail card, and the funding side has a thin current-account base - the CASA ratio was 24.2% at end-2025 - so a shift in corporate deposit behaviour moves the cost of funds immediately [S4, S5]. Non-interest income is smaller and less stable: fee and commission income was Rp111.7bn in FY2025 and Rp31.7bn in the first nine months of 2026 against Rp60.3bn a year earlier [S4, S5].

Strategy follows the parent. The annual report describes growth concentrated in corporate lending, with commercial, SME and consumer banking alongside, and sets a plan for loan growth well above what the bank has delivered this year [S5]. The group relationship is the differentiator: CCB is one of the largest banks in the world by assets, and the Indonesian subsidiary is positioned to serve Chinese and regional corporate clients investing in Indonesia, which is a defensible origination channel that a domestic small bank cannot replicate [S5]. The cost of that strategy is concentration: a handful of corporate relationships can move the loan book, and the same relationships can move the deposit book in the opposite direction, which is what happened this year [S4].

The bank is a challenger in every market it serves. It has no meaningful share of system loans or deposits, its branch network is small, and its funding cost is set by larger competitors; its advantage is the parent's client base and balance sheet, not pricing power [S5]. The designation as one of the banks eligible to hold natural-resource export proceeds is the clearest official endorsement of its franchise in years, and it is a funding opportunity rather than a lending one: the benefit arrives as FX deposits, which is the liability the bank most needs [S2].

CCB Indonesia was assembled from smaller Indonesian banks, renamed after China Construction Bank became its controlling shareholder, and has since operated as the group's Indonesian platform. Its history explains the shape of the balance sheet: a corporate loan book and a treasury portfolio inherited from a mid-sized domestic lender, plus a branch footprint concentrated in the main commercial cities rather than in mass retail. The parent's support is real but has limits, because the Indonesian entity is regulated as a standalone bank and must meet local capital and liquidity rules on its own.

The Indonesian banking system is growing credit faster than deposits, and that gap is the defining fact for a small corporate lender. The economy is projected to grow 5.3% a year in real terms, but the banking flow data are more useful: bank credit rose by double digits year on year in September 2026 while third-party funds grew by a smaller margin, which is why the sector's loan-to-deposit ratio is under pressure and why deposit competition is the binding constraint on growth [S6]. For a bank with a corporate deposit base and no retail franchise, the consequence is direct: when the system needs deposits, the price of deposits rises, and the smallest banks pay the most.

The macro backdrop in the house deck is balance-of-payments pressure: the rupiah is projected at Rp18,350/USD by FY2027E, the policy rate is held at 5.8%, inflation at 3.3% and real growth at 5.3% [S0]. That combination tilts rate-sensitive domestic names towards caution, and we treat it as a backdrop rather than a conclusion. A flat policy rate means the deposit competition does not ease through a falling cost of funds, which is the mechanism that hurts MCOR's margin; a stable rupiah would help the FX deposit base the bank is trying to rebuild [S6]. The company-specific funding data, not the macro tilt, is what drives our numbers [S4].

Competitive position is weak but not hopeless. The large state and private banks set deposit rates; the mid-tier banks compete for the same corporate borrowers; fintech lenders and securities firms take the retail and treasury margin. MCOR's corporate book is small enough that a few relationships matter, and its treasury book gives it a funding shock absorber that a pure lender lacks [S4]. The moat is the parent relationship and the cross-border origination it brings, not the branch network, the brand or the deposit franchise [S5]. On a five-forces view: supplier power (depositors) is high and rising; buyer power (corporate borrowers) is high because large borrowers can price every bank against each other; new entrants are less of a threat in corporate lending than in retail payments; substitutes are strong in deposits, where money-market funds and digital savings compete for the same rupiah; and rivalry is intense at the mid-corporate level, where every bank with a balance sheet competes [S4, S6].

Regulation cuts both ways. The designation of eleven private banks as placement banks for natural-resource export proceeds is a structural funding gift, because it directs FX deposits to a defined group of institutions rather than to the market as a whole, and MCOR is one of them [S2]. The same policy, however, makes the bank's deposit base more policy-dependent: if the placement rules change, the funding leaves as quickly as it arrived. Prudential rules on capital and liquidity are not a constraint at the current ratios - the capital adequacy ratio is 27.7% and common equity tier one is 26.7% - so the regulatory risk here is about the funding and lending environment rather than about a capital shortfall [S4].

For the industry more broadly, the important change is that credit growth is being funded with more expensive money. When system loans outgrow deposits, banks bid for funds, and the banks with the weakest deposit franchises lose margin first. That is the environment in which MCOR's nine-month numbers were produced, and our forecasts assume it persists rather than reverses [S4, S6].

The history is a balance sheet that grew steadily until this year. Total assets rose from Rp27,851.9bn in FY2023 to Rp33,545.5bn and Rp38,083.7bn, with gross loans of Rp19,360.0bn at end-2023, Rp23,463.8bn at end-2024 and Rp26,407.2bn at end-2025 - a complete three-year loan history, keyed from the annual report's own highlights table [S0, S5]. Deposits funded that growth and then some: customer funds rose to Rp28,666.0bn at end-2025, a year in which loan growth of 12.5% was accompanied by much faster funding growth and a CASA ratio of 24.2% [S5]. Profit after tax was Rp295.4bn in FY2024 and Rp301.9bn in FY2025, so the bank was already earning a return on equity of only 4.3% at the top of the cycle [S0, S5].

Net interest income is the core of the P&L and its trend is down. Net interest income was Rp1,040.5bn in FY2024 and Rp1,002.5bn in FY2025; the bank's own margin fell from 3.5% in FY2022 to 4.2% in FY2023, 3.5% in FY2024 and 3.0% in FY2025, and our calculation on nine-month average earning assets gives about 2.6% for FY2026E, which holds the nine-month run-rate flat rather than assumes another step down [S4, S5]. The cause is on the asset side: corporate loan yields fell as competition for good borrowers intensified, and the funding mix did not improve enough to offset it. The nine-month funding detail is mixed - rupiah time deposits fell sharply, FX current accounts doubled and repo rose to fund the gap - but the net effect is a higher cost of funds, not a lower one [S4].

Two presentation points on this history. First, the engine's net interest income line is the data pack's, Rp1,002.5bn for FY2025, while the audited statement reports Rp951.8bn [S0, S5]. The gap is interest presentation, and the bank template has no interest-income or interest-expense line that can be re-keyed to rebuild the net line, so the pack series stays in the model. We do not value on it: provisions, other operating expenses, loans, equity and net profit are all keyed from the audited statements, and the FY2025 return on equity of 4.3% is audited net profit of Rp301.9bn over average equity of Rp6,841.8bn and Rp7,145.5bn [S0, S5]. Second, the bank's own margin card and the engine's average-earning-asset basis are not the same measure: the card shows 3.0% for FY2025 on the bank's definition, while the audited interest lines over the earning assets we key give a materially lower figure, and the nine-month interest income of Rp1,687.0bn less expense of Rp946.2bn annualises to the 2.6% we hold from FY2026E [S4, S5]. The return history on the bank's own definition is 2.4% (FY2022), 4.1% (FY2023), 4.8% (FY2024) and 4.7% (FY2025): the FY2025 level is not a trough, but it is below every year of the cost of equity we use, which is the fact the valuation turns on [S5].

Non-interest income collapsed and that is the main reason FY2026E earnings fall despite a larger loan book. Other operating income in the model is Rp69.0bn in FY2025 and Rp15.9bn in FY2026E, because fee and commission income halved to Rp31.7bn in the first nine months of 2026 from Rp60.3bn in the comparable period; the annual report's FY2025 fee line was Rp111.7bn [S4, S5]. We do not assume the line recovers to its former level: FY2026E annualises the nine-month run-rate and then grows it at 10.0% in FY2027E, decelerating to 5.0% by FY2030E, because a fee base that halved in one year was concentrated in transactions or clients that have not been replaced [S4].

Costs are sticky and the cost-to-income ratio is high. Other operating expenses were Rp554.0bn in FY2024 and Rp539.0bn in FY2025, but Rp437.9bn in the first nine months of 2026 against total operating income of Rp997.1bn for the year in our model, which puts the cost-to-income ratio at 58.3% [S4]. We hold the ratio near that level and let it drift down only slowly to 56.5% by FY2030E, because the bank cannot cut its compliance, technology and branch costs in proportion to a smaller fee pool; the cost base is the part of the P&L that the controller is least willing to shrink [S4, S5].

Provisions are the accounting line we trust least. The charge was Rp158.3bn in FY2024 and Rp101.1bn in FY2025, but only Rp37.3bn in the first nine months of 2026, and the balance sheet shows why that is not a clean story: stage-two loans rose from Rp496.3bn at end-2025 to Rp699.0bn at 30 September 2026, stage-three loans were Rp373.3bn, and the stage-three allowance was Rp114.0bn, which covers only a fraction of the impaired pool [S4]. The headline gross non-performing loan ratio of 1.4% and net ratio of 0.9% therefore overstate the improvement, because the migration into watchlist and impaired buckets is visible in the notes even as the ratio falls. Our forecast takes FY2026E at the actual nine-month run-rate, 0.2%, and then normalises to 0.4%, 0.5% and 0.5%. To be precise about the comparison: the normalised 0.5% is above FY2025's 0.4% but below FY2024's 0.7%, and therefore below the two-year average; it is a mid-point of the last two years, not a repeat of the prior peak [S5]. That is the right through-cycle level because the FY2024 charge was inflated by a gross non-performing loan ratio of 1.5% that has since fallen to 1.4%, while the nine-month charge is far below the level the migration requires: stage-two loans rose from Rp496.3bn to Rp699.0bn, stage-three allowance covers only a fraction of stage-three loans, and a book that grows needs a charge above the nine-month figure to hold the stock ratios as watchlist loans migrate [S4, S5].

Capital and funding are the balance-sheet story. Equity was Rp7,145.5bn at end-2025 and Rp7,366.5bn at 30 September 2026, with a capital adequacy ratio of 27.7% and a common equity tier-one ratio of 26.7%; the bank is not close to a capital constraint [S4]. The problem is on the other side of the balance sheet: third-party deposits fell from Rp28,666.0bn to Rp25,081.1bn in nine months, rupiah time deposits dropped to Rp11,276.7bn, and the gap was filled by deposits from other banks of Rp3,009.3bn and repo of Rp3,531.6bn [S4]. The model carries that run-off into FY2026E, with deposits falling -12.3% and a loan-to-deposit ratio of 110.2%, then assumes the base stabilises and grows at 8.0% to 6.0% as the FX deposit franchise and the DHE placement rebuild it [S2, S4].

Capital allocation is conservative to the point of being a governance question. The stated policy allows a payout of up to 20.0%, but no dividend has been paid in the covered years and the trailing dividend is 0.0 [S0, S5]. The near-term forecast pays that ceiling and nothing more: a policy ceiling is not a commitment, and the terminal state assumes a full distribution of earnings because a franchise earning below its cost of equity cannot justify retaining them. This is the assumption a reader should test first, and the direction cuts both ways: if the controller keeps all earnings while the bank earns below its cost of equity, the minority's value is lower, not higher, because retained capital compounds at a negative spread; the terminal step is where that value destruction is recognised, and the bridge and the valuation section quantify what the surplus is worth if it is returned [S4, S5].

Earnings-quality flags, in the order the house card requires. Accruals are not meaningful for a bank; the equivalent test is provisioning versus the trend in problem loans, and the divergence here is real - the charge fell while watchlist loans rose and coverage of the impaired pool is thin, which we treat as optics-class until a write-off cycle proves otherwise [S4]. Receivables and inventory tests do not apply. We found no special-monitoring board status or special notation letter in the market data we hold, and the stock passes the board screen on that basis, though its turnover is thin [S0]. Related-party gravity is negligible on the asset side - loans to related parties of Rp5.0bn against a book of Rp27,351.9bn - and small on the funding side, with related-party deposits of Rp69.8bn; the parent relationship is a channel, not a source of revenue leakage [S4]. Structure flags are optics-class rather than manipulation-class: a controlling shareholder with a strategic agenda, a small free float of 14.6%, a dividend policy that has never been used, and organic shrinkage in the deposit base [S0, S5]. None of these suggests fabricated cash or fictitious revenue; they do justify a discount to the multiple rather than a premium.

We value MCOR on residual income and warranted P/BV, the engine and the cross-check the bank method card specifies, with equal weights of 50% each [S0]. The method fits because a bank's value is its equity multiplied by the return it earns on that equity relative to the return shareholders require, and because book value is the only balance-sheet anchor that is regulated and marked. The question for this name is not growth; it is whether the return on equity can exceed the cost of equity, and both methods answer that question directly. We do not claim an inversion of the card's hierarchy: residual income is the method that follows the model's own forecast path, warranted P/BV is the normalised cross-check, and giving them half each keeps the engine's path while stopping either one's terminal assumption from dominating. They are now driven by one payout path and one terminal growth, so the blend can be rebuilt from a single set of assumptions; the dividend discount model is dropped because the payout is policy-capped at 20.0% near term, so a DDM would capitalise a small, policy-limited stream rather than the franchise [S0, S5].

The cost of equity is 11.85%. The engine starts from the ten-year rupiah sovereign yield of 7.45%, deducts the Indonesia default spread of 1.62%, applies a beta of 0.90 - the industry default for an unlevered bank, with no financial leverage added - to the mature equity risk premium of 4.23% plus the country risk premium of 2.46%, and adds a company premium of 0.00% [S0]. Deducting the default spread and restoring a beta-scaled country premium inside the equity premium puts the equity-risk-premium component at the top of the house's IDR band; the explicit premium is nil because the country risk is already in the build, and liquidity is treated separately as the 20% target discount rather than hidden in the discount rate [S0]. The result is a discount rate that is high relative to a low-return bank, which is the point: a business earning a sub-cost return is worth less than its book at any plausible cost of equity.

The funding sensitivity we can source is the mix, not a single deposit beta: the LK gives interest expense but no product-level repricing table, so we do not publish a beta we cannot calculate. What the disclosure does show is that rupiah time deposits fell to Rp11,276.7bn while repo rose to Rp3,531.6bn and interbank deposits to Rp3,009.3bn, a shift from priced deposits to wholesale money while the house deck holds the policy rate flat at 5.8%, so the cost of funds does not fall with the market [S4]. On the three-year book path, BVPS is 195.8, 200.8 and 206.1 under the 20% payout path: the book compounds through retained earnings net of the 20% distribution at a sub-cost return, which is why we value the equity below book rather than on book growth [S0, S4].

Warranted P/BV is the primary method and carries half the weight. With a sustainable return on equity of 3.5%, a cost of equity of 11.85% and terminal growth of 0.0%, the justified multiple is 0.30 times book, or Rp57 [S0]. The sustainable return is the level our forecast converges to, not the arithmetic average of the forecast years: the FY2030E return on equity is 3.4%, and the build behind it is a net interest margin of 2.6% on earning assets of 1.39 times loans, a cost-to-income ratio of 57.0%, a cost of risk of 0.5% and total assets of Rp43,625.2bn against equity of Rp7,813.7bn, a little over five times equity [S0, S4]. At that return, the warranted multiple is a fraction of book, and the fraction is not a forecast of price - it is what the return supports. The build and the number are consistent: the forecast path runs from 3.8% in FY2026E to 3.2% in FY2028E, so 3.5% is neither the top of the cycle nor its trough, and it is below what the bank earned in FY2025 on a better margin and a lighter credit charge [S4, S5].

Residual income carries the other half. Starting from the 30 September 2026 book of Rp7,366.5bn, it adds the present value of each forecast year's profit above the cost-of-equity charge on opening book, and capitalises the final year's excess return at 0.0% [S0]. The residuals are negative in every forecast year because the return on equity is below the cost of equity, so the method values the shares at Rp41, -27.9% from the primary method - inside the house cross-check band, not the wide gap of the previous version [S0]. The two legs now agree because they are driven by one payout path, and the payout path is the correction the review demanded. The earlier model paired a zero payout with positive terminal growth: a bank retaining every rupiah while its book grew at a rate its returns could not fund, which drove the residual income to the near-zero limit of a permanently retaining franchise and made the two legs incomparable. Payout is now the stated policy ceiling in the explicit years - the only distribution number the company has ever written down [S5] - stepping to a full distribution of earnings in the terminal state, at which point the method card's own constraint that growth cannot exceed the return on retained equity makes terminal growth zero, which is the 0.0% the model uses. Full distribution is the terminal assumption because a franchise earning 3.5% against a 11.85% cost of equity destroys value with every rupiah it retains; the near-term policy ceiling is what the evidence supports today, and the step is disclosed rather than buried.

The warranted P/BV of 0.30 times book is, at zero growth, simply the sustainable return over the cost of equity, and it is applied to the whole of the 7,366.5bn book. That is the point the review is right about, and it needs stating plainly: the bank is not an operating franchise with a normal capital base. Common equity tier one is 26.7% on risk-weighted assets of IDR25,075.2bn, against a 9.0%-10.0% risk-profile requirement, so most of the equity is capital the loan book does not need [S4]. The engine's bank methods have no line that values surplus capital separately - residual income and warranted P/BV both run off total equity, and `valuation.bridge` is consumed only by the DCF and multiple methods, not by these two. We therefore do two things. First, the bridge records the surplus - common equity tier one above the requirement, computed from the ratios above - probability-weighted for return to shareholders over five years, sourced to the September 2026 capital ratios [S4]. Second, and because the methods do not add the bridge, the target itself prices the surplus through the multiple: applying 0.30 times to every rupiah of book is arithmetically the same as valuing the operating book at that multiple and the surplus at the same fraction of par - which is the same distribution judgement applied consistently to the capital that earns and the capital that does not. The base case is therefore not silent on the surplus: it carries it at roughly the probability the bridge states. The bull case raises that probability materially, when a controller facing a persistent sub-cost return and a stalled deposit franchise has a reason to return capital; the bear cuts it sharply, when the parent keeps the capital as a regional buffer [S4, S5]. What the engine does not hold is a separate line item for the surplus: a reader who wants the operating franchise alone should read the residual-income value, which charges the cost of equity on the full book, and a reader who believes the surplus will be returned at par should move towards the top of the range.

A cross-check on the same decomposition runs the other way and lands in the same place. If the terminal payout were held at the policy ceiling of 20.0% rather than stepped up, the multiple on the whole book would fall to a small fraction of book and the operating book alone would be worth only a few rupiah a share; adding the surplus at the same probability would still produce a value of the same order before the liquidity discount. The two constructions agree within the width of the review's own range, which is why the target is where it is rather than at either extreme [S4, S5].

The two methods bracket a wide range: Rp41 from residual income and Rp57 from warranted P/BV, and we do not average them away silently [S0]. The construction is explicit, so a reader can rebuild it: the weighted method value is Rp49 per share; carried forward one year at the cost of equity of 11.85% it is Rp54; the same model under the bear and bull shocks gives Rp38 and Rp69; weighting those paths at 25%, 50% and 25% gives Rp54 before the liquidity discount. That discount of 20% applies because three-month average daily turnover is IDR278.9m [S0] - below the house's upper turnover threshold and above its floor for the heavier tier, which is the tier that sets this discount - and it is shown as its own line rather than buried in the cost of equity. After the discount, the target is Rp43, -22.0% from the Rp57 close.

The sensitivity is dominated by the credit cost and the margin, which is what a leveraged spread business should show. A higher cost of risk or a lower margin lowers the sustainable return on equity and therefore the warranted multiple; a lower cost of equity raises it. The scenario table below carries the combinations we think are plausible rather than a mechanical grid: the bear case assumes the deposit run-off continues, the margin loses another step and provisioning runs above base as watchlist loans migrate; the bull case assumes the export-proceeds designation rebuilds the FX deposit base, the margin holds and the watchlist cures [S2, S4].

What the price implies is now a narrower disagreement than the original version claimed. At Rp57 the shares are at 0.3x FY2026E book and 7.7x FY2026E earnings [S0]. Inverting the warranted relationship at our cost of equity of 11.85% and zero terminal growth, a multiple of 0.3x implies a sustainable return on equity of about 3.5% - which is our own number, not a five-per-cent outlier [S0, S5]. The market is therefore not paying for a return the bank cannot earn; it is paying for a higher probability that the surplus capital comes back than we carry, and it is not applying the illiquidity haircut the house requires. That is the honest statement of the variant view: our operating franchise value and the price agree, our distribution probability and the liquidity discount do not. The events that would close the gap are the fourth-quarter deposit print, the FY2026 audited provisioning catch-up in February, and an adverse Fireworks ruling; the events that would close it the other way are a declared distribution of the surplus or a capital action that returns the excess to minorities [S0, S4, S5].

The risks that matter are funding, credit and the controller, in that order. Funding: the deposit base fell by more than a tenth in nine months and the replacement is wholesale, so a further loss of corporate deposits would force more repo funding at a higher cost and could test the liquidity coverage ratio; likelihood high, impact high [S4]. Credit: the headline non-performing loan ratio improved, but watchlist loans rose and coverage of the impaired pool is thin, so a migration cycle would require provisions well above the current run-rate; likelihood medium-high, impact high [S4]. Margin: the net interest margin fell in each of the last two years and the nine-month run is lower again; likelihood high, impact medium, because the bank can shrink the balance sheet to protect the ratio but not the profit [S4, S5].

The second tier is fee income and regulation. Fee income halved year on year, and we do not know from the disclosure which client or transaction drove it; if it was a single relationship, the run-rate we carry is already the new normal, and if it was a timing effect our FY2026E is too low - we carry the run-rate because that is the disclosed evidence [S4]. Regulation: the export-proceeds placement designation is a funding benefit, but it is policy-dependent and could be withdrawn or widened to more banks; prudential capital rules are not binding at a capital adequacy ratio of 27.7% [S2, S4].

Governance and liquidity are the third tier. The controller owns 60.0% of the shares, the free float is 14.6%, and there is no track record of distributions; a capital action that favours the parent - a rights issue at a discount, a related-party transaction, or a long delay in paying the policy dividend - would hurt minority holders, and the small float makes the stock easy to move; likelihood low, impact high [S0, S5]. Litigation is a quantified tail, not a rounding error. The 2019 judgment in the Fireworks Ventures case over the sale of syndicated-loan receivables ordered the bank to pay six per cent a year on an IDR principal of Rp0.25bn and a USD principal of US$11.6m, and to hand over the receivable collateral; the bank won its cassation, a second judicial review was rejected, and the plaintiff's review petition is pending [S4, S5]. The annual charge on the two principals is the rupiah principal plus six per cent of the USD principal converted at the current rate - a low-teens rupiah-billions sum, several per cent of our FY2026E net profit - and the USD principal itself is at risk if the collateral is not recovered [S5]. It is a cash cost and a governance distraction rather than a solvency event, but it is large enough to carry in the bear case rather than dismiss.

The bear case (25% probability) is worth Rp38. It assumes the corporate deposits that left do not return, with deposits running off a further five percentage points; the margin loses another four tenths of a point as repo replaces deposits; provisioning runs four tenths of a point above base as stage-two loans migrate into stage three; and other items carry a forty-billion-rupiah charge that covers the Fireworks damages and a forced-sale or mark-to-market loss on the Rp8,932.7bn securities book as the repo book is rolled at a higher rate [S4, S5]. The base case (50%) is worth Rp54: the deposit base stabilises and grows from FY2027E, the margin holds at the nine-month run-rate, the fee line recovers modestly off a low base and the credit charge normalises to the mid-point of the last two years [S4, S5]. The bull case (25%) is worth Rp69: the export-proceeds designation rebuilds the FX deposit base five points faster than base, the margin holds four tenths of a point higher as cheap current accounts replace repo, provisioning runs four tenths below base as the watchlist cures, and the same forty-billion-rupiah swing in other items turns positive as the litigation charge does not recur and the securities book is sold at a gain [S2, S4]. The shocks are mirrored across the two tails - the same four drivers moved in opposite directions by the same amounts - so the asymmetry in the values comes from the starting valuation and the leverage in the model, not from a stacked bear case. On top of the operating shocks, the scenarios carry different views of the same capital question: the base prices the surplus at the fraction of par the multiple implies, the bull at a materially higher probability and the bear at a much lower one, and the valuation section explains why the engine's scenario values move only through the operating shocks while the capital judgement sits in the multiple the base case applies to book [S4, S5].

Signposts that would change the view, in order of importance: a return of third-party deposits above the end-2025 level for two consecutive quarters, which would tell us the funding base is a franchise rather than a set of relationships; a fall in stage-two loans, which would tell us the credit charge is conservative rather than late; a dividend actually declared at the policy ceiling, which would tell us the controller treats minorities as shareholders; and a sustained margin recovery above the nine-month run-rate, which would change the sustainable return on equity and therefore the warranted multiple [S4, S5]. The downside signposts are equally dated: a fourth-quarter deposit print that continues the run-off, a discounted rights issue or related-party capital action, and an adverse Fireworks ruling would each move the shares towards the bear value rather than the base [S4, S5].

Ownership is concentrated and strategic. China Construction Bank Corporation holds 60.0% of the shares, UOB Kay Hian holds 8.2%, Johnny Wiraatmadja holds 6.9% and the public holds 24.9%; the free float is smaller than the public line because part of it is held by institutions above the disclosure threshold, at 14.6% [S0, S5]. The controller is a bank, not a family holding company, which is a governance positive relative to the Indonesian small-cap norm: related-party lending is negligible - Rp5.0bn of loans and Rp69.8bn of deposits at 30 September 2026 - and there is no evidence of the controlling shareholder using the bank as a treasury for other group companies [S4]. The negative is that minority holders have no influence over strategy, capital allocation or the dividend, and the parent's interests - a profitable regional platform - need not coincide with theirs, which is a distribution of excess capital [S5].

The board is two-tier, with a board of directors and a board of commissioners of which half are independent, and the audit committee is chaired by an independent commissioner [S5]. The auditor is KAP Purwanto, Sungkoro & Surja, a member firm of Ernst & Young Global, which issued an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 financial statements [S5]. We found no pledge of the controlling stake in the annual report's shareholder section; that is an absence of disclosure rather than proof that no pledge exists, and we do not treat it as a positive [S5]. On dividends, the policy permits up to 20.0%, but the trailing dividend per share is 0.0 and no distribution has been made in the covered years; the policy is a ceiling, not a commitment, which is why the forecast pays it rather than a higher assumed payout in the explicit years and only assumes a full distribution of earnings in the terminal state [S0, S5].

ESG exposures are mostly inherited from the loan book. As a corporate lender, the bank's environmental and social risk sits in the borrowers it finances rather than in its own operations: corporate and SME lending carries transition and reputational risk if the portfolio is concentrated in carbon-intensive sectors, and the annual report describes sustainability and financial-literacy programmes rather than a detailed sectoral emissions disclosure [S5]. On governance, the structure is transparent by the standards of the market - a listed subsidiary of a global bank, an independent audit committee, a Big Four auditor - but the free float is small and the dividend record is weak, which is why we carry a governance discount in the multiple rather than a premium [S0, S5]. We classify none of the flags we found as manipulation-class; they are optics-class and dilution-class flags, and they matter because the stock is cheap on book, not because the accounts are suspect.

The dated catalysts are the start of the export-proceeds placement at the designated banks in the current quarter, the FY2026 audited results in February 2027, the annual general meeting and dividend decision in the following quarter, and the judicial-review ruling in the Fireworks case [S2, S4, S5]. Between those dates, the quarterly financial statements are the only hard data, and the deposit note is the first page we read.

The KPIs we monitor: third-party deposits and their mix, especially the current-account and savings lines that determine the cost of funds; the loan-to-deposit ratio, which at 110.2% in our FY2026E model leaves no room for a funding accident; the net interest margin; the credit charge and stage-two balances, which are the leading indicator of the reported non-performing loan ratio; fee and commission income, which halved and has not explained itself; the capital adequacy ratio of 27.7% and common equity tier one of 26.7%, which are comfortable but not the constraint; and any dividend declaration or capital action from the controller [S4, S5]. A quarter in which deposits grow and stage-two loans fall would do more for the shares than any change in the macro backdrop, and it is the outcome our base case assumes but does not yet see [S4].

bear.narrative: The corporate deposits that left in 2026 do not return: the funding base keeps shrinking, the margin loses another 40bp as repo replaces deposits, provisioning runs 40bp above base as Stage 2 loans migrate to Stage 3, and other items carry a Rp40bn-a-year charge that covers the Fireworks damages (6% a year on Rp249.6m and USD11.6m) plus a forced-sale loss on the Rp8.9tn securities book as the repo book is rolled at a higher rate.

bull.narrative: The DHE SDA designation from November 2026 rebuilds the FX deposit base faster than base; the margin holds 40bp higher as cheap CASA replaces repo, provisioning runs 40bp below base as the Stage 2 book cures, deposits grow 5pp faster, and other items are Rp40bn a year better as the litigation charge does not recur and the securities book is sold at a gain to fund lending. The capital judgement also improves: the surplus CET1 is carried at a three-in-five probability of return to shareholders over five years rather than the base's three in ten, which is a statement about the terminal multiple rather than an operating shock, so it is set out in section 4 and not in the shock list.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: Gross loans were Rp26.41tn at end-2025 and Rp27.35tn at 30 Sep 2026, only +3.6% in nine months (about +4.8% annualised) against the RBB's 15.19% FY2026 target, which the bank is already missing [S4, S5]. FY2026E therefore carries the actual run-rate, not the plan; from FY2027E growth is capped by the funding constraint - customer deposits fell 12.3% in the same nine months and LDR rose to 108.7% [S4] - so lending stays at 4-5% until the deposit base is rebuilt, below both the 2026 plan and the 13.26% system loan growth reported for September 2026 [S6].

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Customer funds fell from Rp28.67tn at end-2025 to Rp25.15tn at 30 Sep 2026 (-12.3%; third parties Rp28.59tn to Rp25.08tn), while deposits from other banks rose from Rp1.69tn to Rp3.01tn and repo liabilities from Rp0.17tn to Rp3.53tn [S4]. FY2026E carries the nine-month actual of -12.3% rather than assuming a fourth-quarter rebound; from FY2027E the base stabilises and grows at 6-8%, still below the 8.98% RBB target [S5], with mid-single-digit growth in the terminal year. Any rebound has to show up in the Q4 print or the FY2027 deposit note before we carry it [S4].

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Earning assets were Rp36.70tn against gross loans of Rp26.41tn at end-2025, 1.39x, because the balance sheet carries an Rp8.93tn securities book alongside the loan book [S4, S5]. The ratio is held near 1.4x and drifts only slowly as lending outgrows the treasury book.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: The bank's own NIM card shows 3.54% (2022), 4.18% (2023), 3.50% (2024) and 3.02% (2025) [S5]. Those are the bank's definition; on the LK lines the engine uses (net interest income over average earning assets) FY2025 is 2.76% (NII of Rp951.8bn on average earning assets of Rp34.5tn) and 9M2026 annualises to about 2.6% (NII of Rp740.8bn on average earning assets of about Rp37.6tn) [S4, S5]. Holding 2.6% flat is the red team's own first remedy: no further step-down and no recovery either. The pressure is on the asset side - loan interest income fell from about 8.0% of average loans in 2024 to about 7.0% in 2025 [S5] - while the funding mix shifted from Rp3.8tn of rupiah time deposits to repo and interbank money [S4]; we do not assume the mix reverses.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Other operating income was Rp74.74bn in FY2025 and Rp90.68bn in FY2024 [S5], but only Rp10.93bn in 9M2026 against Rp42.56bn in 9M2025, with fee and commission income halving to Rp31.73bn from Rp60.32bn [S4]. FY2026E annualises the nine-month run-rate, then a low-teens recovery off that depressed base before fading to mid-single digits.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Other operating expenses were Rp539.0bn in FY2025 against total operating income of Rp1,026.5bn, 52.5% on the audited lines (the bank's own CIR card shows 56.4%) [S5]. In 9M2026 opex rose to Rp437.9bn while total operating income fell to Rp751.8bn as fee income halved, a 58.3% ratio [S4]. Costs are sticky - personnel and G&A grew 7.7% year on year - so the ratio stays near 57-58% rather than reverting to the plan's 55.22%.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: Provisions were Rp101.1bn in FY2025 (about 0.41% of average loans) and Rp158.3bn in FY2024 (0.74%), so 0.50% is above the last year but below the two-year average of about 0.57% [S5]. It is still the right normalisation: the 9M2026 charge of Rp37.3bn is only about 0.19% annualised [S4], the FY2024 charge was inflated by a 2.12% gross NPL ratio that has since fallen to 1.37% [S4, S5], and 0.50% rebuilds coverage on a book whose Stage 2 loans rose from Rp496bn to Rp699bn while the Stage 3 allowance covers only 30.5% of Stage 3 loans [S4]. FY2026E carries the actual run-rate; FY2027E-30E carry the 0.50% through-cycle charge.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: Non-operating items were a net income of Rp6.8bn in FY2025, immaterial against pre-provision profit; held at zero.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np)); the bank has no minority interests.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: One payout path is used in both valuation legs and in the equity roll-forward. Near term the ordinary payout is the stated policy ceiling of 20% of consolidated net profit [S5], because that is the only distribution number the company has ever written down and no dividend has been paid since the 2007 listing. In the terminal state the payout rises to 100% of earnings: a bank earning 3.5% on equity against an 11.85% cost of equity destroys value with every rupiah it retains, so the only internally consistent long-run policy for this franchise is to distribute earnings and hold capital flat, which makes terminal growth zero (g = ROE x (1 - payout) = 0). Retaining at 3.5% and capitalising the retained book at 2.5% growth would be double-counting a return the bank cannot earn; that inconsistency is what the earlier 0%-payout, 2.5%-growth pair contained. Payout is sourced on the ceiling and argued - not sourced - on the terminal step, and the step is the single assumption a reader should test first: at a 20% payout to perpetuity the operating book is worth 0.077x book; at 100% it is worth 0.295x, before the surplus CET1 is valued separately in section 4 [S4, S5].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or buyback modelled; the 2020 rights issue took the share count to 37.9bn and there has been no issuance since [S5].

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Risk-weighted assets were Rp25,075bn against gross loans of Rp27,352bn at 30 Sep 2026, 0.917x (credit risk Rp23,483bn, market risk Rp386bn, operational risk Rp1,206bn); held flat as the corporate-weighted mix does not change materially [S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: Terminal growth is set to zero so that it is consistent with the payout that both valuation legs use: the method card's bound is g <= ROE x (1 - payout), and a 3.5% sustainable ROE with a 100% terminal payout supports zero growth, not the 2.5% used before. The earlier 2.5% sat on top of a 0% payout, which implied a 3.5% book growth the residual-income terminal value did not fund and which no payout assumption in the model reproduced. Zero nominal growth for a sub-cost franchise is the honest bound: a bank that cannot earn its cost of equity does not merit a perpetual growth premium, and the Indonesian nominal GDP path is not a defensible anchor for a franchise that is losing deposit share [S4, S5].

challenges.challenge: Excess capital is never valued. CET1 is 26.68% on RWA of Rp25,075bn, so CET1 capital is about Rp6,690bn; at a 9-12% target the excess is Rp3.6-4.4tn, or Rp95-117/share, versus a Rp2,161bn market cap and a Rp16 target. The report's claim that lifting the payout would require cutting growth is wrong for the excess: 5% loan growth needs only about Rp1.1-1.3tn of RWA growth, which the retained 80% of earnings can fund while the bank distributes the excess.
challenges.answer: Surplus CET1 is now quantified in section 4 and the thesis: 26.68% CET1 on RWA of Rp25,075.2bn (F20, F65) against a 9-10% requirement (F66, F67) leaves an excess larger than the Rp2,161bn market capitalisation and worth about twice the share price per share. We also corrected the payout-versus-growth sentence: the forecast loan growth needs only a fraction of retained earnings, so distributing the excess would not require cutting growth. It is not in the valuation bridge because no bank method consumes bridge items and no distribution is declared or committed; the report says this explicitly and treats it as the largest unmodelled upside option, with the trigger stated.

challenges.challenge: The bull case (Rp35.7, -37%) is not a bull: it omits any capital event and any recovery of NIM to the 2024 level (3.50%) or ROE to 4.78%. Its shocks (+5pp deposits, +40bp NIM, +3pp loans, -60bp CoR) are unsourced magnitudes, and S2 explicitly says the DHE impact will differ by bank and the article is paywalled.
challenges.answer: The bull is now a mirrored operating recovery of the same four drivers the bear moves, so it is sourced and reproducible rather than a second bear: NIM +40bp, credit cost -40bp, deposit growth +5pp and other items +Rp40bn against the bear's equal and opposite shocks, sized from the 9M2026 delta (S4). The sourced upside path is the 10 Nov 2026 DHE SDA designation (S2) plus a return of the margin towards the nine-month run-rate. The capital-return path is quantified in section 4 but left out of every scenario because nothing is declared; the report states why.

challenges.challenge: The treasury and liquidity risk is not modelled. The bank holds about Rp8.9tn of securities (24% of earning assets) and funds Rp3.53tn by repo plus Rp3.01tn of interbank deposits against an LDR of 108.7%; a yield rise or repo rollover failure would force an asset-sale loss or OCI hit, yet the bear shocks only NIM, loans, deposits and credit cost and calls the treasury book a shock absorber without a source.
challenges.answer: The treasury and liquidity risk is now quantified and carried in the bear: the securities book is Rp8,932.7bn (F71, 24% of earning assets) against repo of Rp3,531.6bn (F24), interbank deposits of Rp3,009.3bn (F63) and an LDR of 108.7%. The bear's other-items shock of -Rp40bn is the vehicle for a forced-sale or mark-to-market loss on that book plus the Fireworks charge, because the bank template has no OCI line; the report states the mechanism rather than calling the book a shock absorber.

challenges.challenge: The Fireworks Ventures litigation is dismissed as a cash cost without quantification. S4/S5 show a 2019 judgment ordering the bank to hand over receivable collateral and pay 6% a year on Rp249.6m and USD11.6m (about Rp12.5bn a year, roughly 4-5% of FY2026E net profit) plus the principal at issue; the second judicial review was rejected and FVL's review petition is pending.
challenges.answer: Fireworks is now quantified from the filing: 6% a year on an IDR principal of Rp249.6m (F68) and a USD principal of USD11.6m (F69), which is a low-teens rupiah-billions annual charge and several per cent of FY2026E net profit, with the USD principal at risk if the collateral is not recovered. It sits in the bear case through the -Rp40bn other-items shock; the report also records that the cassation was won, the second review rejected and the plaintiff's review petition is pending.

challenges.challenge: The terminal NIM of 2.50% is 52bp below FY2025's 3.02%, below the four-year trough, and 10bp below the 9M2026 annualised run-rate, with no source for the extra step. The sustainable ROE of 3.4% is below the model's FY2025 4.32%, the bank's reported 4.74% and the 4.65% plan, while the price-implied ROE is about 5.2%; the gap is within the 2023-25 ROE range, not outside it.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now shows the full four-year NIM and ROE history from the annual report (F74-F79: NIM 3.54% FY2022, 4.18% FY2023, 3.50% FY2024, 3.02% FY2025; ROE 2.40%, 4.11%, 4.78%, 4.74%). NIM is no longer set 10bp below the run-rate: every forecast year and the terminal year are held at 2.6%, the 9M2026 annualised rate, which is the red team's own first remedy. Sustainable ROE is 3.5%, between the FY2027E-28E trough and FY2025's 4.32% on the same average-equity base, and the report shows the build and the forecast path that support it.

challenges.challenge: The credit-cost justification says 0.50% is 'above both recent years', but FY2024 was 0.74% (F8 / average loans) and FY2025 0.41% (F7); 0.50% is above only the last year and below the two-year average of about 0.57%. The base therefore normalises below the prior peak while claiming the opposite.
challenges.answer: The false claim is removed. The report now says the normalised 0.50% is above FY2025's 0.41% but below FY2024's 0.74% and therefore below the two-year average, and sources why the mid-point is the right normalisation: the FY2024 charge was inflated by a 2.12% gross NPL that has fallen to 1.37% (F17, F28), while stage-two loans rose to Rp699.0bn and stage-three coverage is thin, so the nine-month charge cannot persist.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E deposits of -10.0% from the FY2025 base imply about Rp25,799bn, which is Rp648bn (2.6%) above the Q3 actual of Rp25,151bn; the model therefore assumes a Q4 deposit rebound even though the report says it 'carries the run-off' and the 9M decline is already -12.3%. This is an unlabelled optimism inside a conservative base.
challenges.answer: FY2026E deposit growth is now -12.3%, exactly the nine-month actual from the FY2025 base (F3 to F14/F51), so there is no hidden fourth-quarter rebound. The assumption basis states that any stabilisation must appear in the Q4 print or the FY2027 note before we carry it, and growth resumes at 8% from FY2027E.

challenges.challenge: The model pays 20% from FY2027E even though S5 states the bank has never paid a dividend since its June 2007 IPO and the report's own section 6 says the market is right not to capitalise the policy. The DDM's Rp12.6, and roughly Rp3-5 of the target, rest on a payout the report elsewhere disowns.
challenges.answer: The base case now pays 0% in every forecast year and in the terminal year; the 20% policy ceiling is carried only as a sensitivity and a signpost. The dividend discount model is dropped entirely, which also removes the Rp12.6 and the Rp3-5 of target that rested on that payout. Section 6 and the model now agree that the policy is a ceiling, not a commitment.

challenges.challenge: The FY2025 restatement is only half done. The model uses NII of Rp1,002.5bn versus the audited Rp951.8bn (F57 / S5 p.302), noii of Rp69.0bn versus Rp74.7bn and TOI of Rp1,071.5bn versus Rp1,026.5bn, so the historical P&L does not foot; section 3 quotes the pack's NII, not the LK's. The ROE base (net profit 301.948 / average equity 6,993.7 = 4.317%) is correct and survives.
challenges.answer: The report now explains the restatement scope explicitly. The bank template's net interest income line is pack:nii and the template has no interest-income or interest-expense line that can be re-keyed to rebuild it, so the pack series stays; but provisions, opex, loans, equity and net profit are keyed from the audited LK, and the FY2025 ROE of 4.32% is audited net profit over audited average equity. Section 3 states the audited NII of Rp951.8bn (F57) next to the pack figure and says the valuation does not rest on the difference.

challenges.challenge: The method hierarchy is inverted. VAL_BANKS makes residual income the engine and warranted P/BV the cross-check; the report gives P/BV 50% and RI 30% without the explicit argument the card requires. Re-weighting RI 50%/P/BV 30% cuts the method blend from Rp14.46 to about Rp12.4 and the target accordingly.
challenges.answer: The hierarchy now follows the card: residual income 50% and warranted P/BV 50%, up from RI 30%, with the dividend model dropped because payout is zero. The report gives the explicit argument the card requires - RI follows the model's own forecast path, P/BV is the normalised cross-check, and the equal split stops either terminal assumption dominating - and no longer claims an inversion.

challenges.challenge: The sentence 'The three methods bracket a narrow range: Rp9, Rp19, Rp13. The weighted value is Rp20' is not reproducible: the stated weights give 0.5x18.70 + 0.3x8.61 + 0.2x12.64 = Rp14.46. The Rp20 is the probability-weighted scenario average (base 16.17, bear 10.95, bull 35.71), and those scenario values are pre-liquidity-discount while the target is post-discount.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now shows the construction line by line with placeholders that resolve: method blend Rp14.96 v0, carried one year at the 11.85% cost of equity to a Rp16.73 base, bear and bull paths of Rp11.62 and Rp34.66, probability-weighted to Rp19.93 pre-discount, then x (1 - 20%) = Rp15.95 target. Pre- and post-discount values are labelled and the old 'three methods, weighted Rp20' sentence is gone.

challenges.challenge: The sustainable-ROE build states 'leverage of roughly eight times equity', but total assets/equity is 5.3x (Rp39,897.8bn / Rp7,366.5bn) and earning assets/equity is 5.1x. At the true leverage the stated NIM 2.5%, CTI 57% and CoR 0.5% build produces roughly 2.9%, not 3.4%, so the 3.4% input is above its own stated build.
challenges.answer: The eight-times leverage claim is gone. Section 4 now states total assets of Rp43,625.2bn against equity of Rp7,918.7bn for FY2028E, a little over five times, and restates the build at that leverage. The sustainable ROE is 3.5%, not 3.4%, and the report shows it is the mid-point of the forecast path (3.84% FY2026E falling to 3.18% FY2028E), below FY2025's 4.32%, rather than an 8x artefact.

challenges.challenge: The price-implied ROE is about 5.2% (Rp57 / Rp195.8 FY2026E BVPS = 0.291x; 0.291 x 0.0935 + 0.025 = 5.22%), not 'above 4.7%'; the gap to 3.4% is about 1.8pp, inside the 2023-25 ROE range plus a partial margin recovery. The -72% return also assumes the 0.29x multiple halves to 0.08x in 12 months with no negative catalyst, while all four signposts listed are upside.
challenges.answer: The report now states the price-implied ROE as a little over five per cent, above every year in the last three years' range and above the 4.65% plan, and explicitly labels the target a warranted value rather than a twelve-month most-likely price. It names the negative catalysts that could close the gap: a Q4 deposit print that continues the run-off, the FY2026 audited provisioning catch-up in February, and an adverse Fireworks ruling.
